knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional reachable set of a solution map
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential reachability of solution-map values along a fixed positive parameter ray.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a reference parameter $y^0$ and a fixed direction $r$, define
\[\mathcal{RP}(y^0;r):=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists\{(x^k,t^k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty},\ t^k>0,\ x^k\in\Psi(y^0+t^kr)\ \forall k,\ (x^k,t^k)\to(x,0)\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The directional reachable set consists of limits of solution values obtained while the parameter approaches the reference point along the fixed positive ray generated by r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\mathcal{RP}(y^0;r)\iff\exists\{(x^k,t^k)\}_{k=1}^{\infty}\text{ satisfying the stated conditions}

children.title: Radial Direction Geometry
children.top_down_role: Directions generated by direct displacement toward reachable points.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_C(\bar x)=\{\lambda(y-\bar x):\lambda\ge 0,\ y\in C\}\).

notation.meaning: radial cone of C at the reference point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the finite-dimensional, fixed-base radial cone convention and defines the positive-scaling hull explicitly.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The radial direction cone of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
R_C(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\text{there exists }t>0\text{ such that }\bar x+tv\in C\}=\{\lambda(y-\bar x):\lambda\ge 0,\ y\in C\}.
\]
A radial direction therefore requires one positive displacement from the fixed base point along its ray to reach \(C\), without requiring the intervening segment to lie in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radial direction is one whose ray from the reference point meets the set at some positive distance.
knowledge_statements.title: Radial Direction Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direction Points and Cosmic Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines positive-scaling directions, their horizon, and the cosmic closure of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $x,x'\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{0\}$, define $\operatorname{dir}x=\operatorname{dir}x'$ exactly when $x'=\lambda x$ for some $\lambda>0$; $\operatorname{dir}0$ is undefined. These direction points correspond bijectively to rays from the origin and form $\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n$. The cosmic space is $\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n:=\mathbb{R}^n\cup\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n$. For $n=1$ its direction points are $-\infty$ and $+\infty$, so $\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}\cong\overline{\mathbb{R}}$; for general $n$, $\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n\neq\overline{\mathbb{R}}^{\,n}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two nonzero vectors have the same direction exactly when one is a positive scalar multiple of the other; zero has no direction. Directions correspond to rays and constitute the horizon of Euclidean space. Adjoining them gives cosmic space. In one dimension this recovers the extended real line, but higher-dimensional cosmic space is not the Cartesian product of extended real lines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n=\mathbb{R}^n\cup\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Horizon and Cosmic Closure of a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates ordinary closure from cosmic closure and identifies the horizon component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For $C\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, let $\operatorname{csm}C$ be its closure in $\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n$ and define its horizon by $\operatorname{hzn}C:=\operatorname{csm}C\cap\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n$. Then $\operatorname{csm}C=\operatorname{cl}C\cup\operatorname{hzn}C$, and $\operatorname{hzn}C$ is closed relative to $\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cosmic closure of a Euclidean set includes both its ordinary closure and all limiting direction points. Those direction limits form the set's horizon, which is relatively closed in the horizon of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{hzn}C=\operatorname{csm}C\cap\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad \operatorname{csm}C=\operatorname{cl}C\cup\operatorname{hzn}C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential Compactness and Boundedness in Cosmic Space
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States compactness for arbitrary ordinary, directional, or mixed sequences and characterizes Euclidean boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every sequence in $\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n$, including any mixture of ordinary and direction points, has a cosmically convergent subsequence. Moreover, a sequence $(x^\nu)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is bounded if and only if none of its cluster points in $\operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n$ belongs to $\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cosmic Euclidean space is sequentially compact: every ordinary, directional, or mixed sequence has a cosmically convergent subsequence. An ordinary Euclidean sequence is bounded exactly when it has no direction point as a cosmic cluster point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{csm}\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is sequentially compact},\qquad (x^\nu)\text{ bounded}\iff\operatorname{Cluster}_{\operatorname{csm}}(x^\nu)\cap\operatorname{hzn}\mathbb{R}^n=\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial-subdifferential representation and bilevel specializations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation when no radial direction has a limit below the reference value, together with pessimistic and optimistic solution-function cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If no \(r\) satisfies \(\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)<\widehat\varphi(x^0)\), then \(\partial_{\mathrm{rad}}\widehat\varphi(x^0)=\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\langle r,d\rangle\leq d\widehat\varphi_{x^0}(r)\ \forall r\text{ with }\widehat\varphi(x^0)=\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)\}\). For \(\varphi_p\), the radial subdifferential is empty if a descending radial limit exists; otherwise \(\partial_{\mathrm{rad}}\varphi_p(x^0)=\{d:\langle d,r\rangle\leq d\varphi_{p,x^0}(r)\ \forall r\}\). For \(\varphi_o\), a descending radial limit cannot occur and the radial subdifferential is given by the analogous inequality over directions whose radial limit equals the reference value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without a descending radial limit, the radial subdifferential consists of vectors dominated by the radial-directional derivative along directions with unchanged radial limit. The pessimistic solution function obeys an empty-or-inequality dichotomy, while the optimistic solution function always falls in the representation case.
assumptions_latex: For the general representation, no \(r\) satisfies \(\widehat\varphi(x^0;r)<\widehat\varphi(x^0)\).
\(\varphi_p\) and \(\varphi_o\) are respectively the pessimistic and optimistic bilevel solution functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated radial-subdifferential representations and pessimistic empty-set alternative hold; the descending-radial-limit alternative is excluded for \(\varphi_o\).

children.title: Feasible-Direction Geometry
children.top_down_role: Directions supported by locally feasible arcs or motions.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(\bar x)=\{v:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ \bar x+[0,\varepsilon]v\subset C\}\).

notation.meaning: cone of feasible directions of C at the reference point
line segment generated by v over the stated interval

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses exact straight-line feasibility, not asymptotic feasibility.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The feasible-direction cone of \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
F_C(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\text{there exists }\varepsilon>0\text{ with }\bar x+tv\in C\text{ for every }t\in[0,\varepsilon]\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\) is feasible when an initial segment of the ray based at \(\bar x\) remains entirely in \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible direction keeps every sufficiently short straight-line displacement from the reference point inside the set.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Direction Geometry

children.title: Reachability Relations Between Direction Systems
children.top_down_role: Inclusion, closure, and local equivalence patterns linking the two systems.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F_C(\bar x)\subset R_C(\bar x)\cap T_C(\bar x)\), with no general inclusion between \(R_C(\bar x)\) and \(T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records only inclusions valid for arbitrary subsets of finite-dimensional space.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every set \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\),
\[
F_C(\bar x)\subset R_C(\bar x)\quad\text{and}\quad F_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x).
\]
Neither \(R_C(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\) nor \(T_C(\bar x)\subset R_C(\bar x)\) holds for arbitrary nonconvex sets. If \(C\) is convex, then \(F_C(\bar x)=R_C(\bar x)\) and \(T_C(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}R_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible directions are radial and contingent. Radial and contingent cones are otherwise incomparable, while convexity restores radial-feasible equality and tangent closure.
knowledge_statements.title: Reachability Relations Between Direction Systems

source_witnesses.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

children.title: Direction-System Separation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric settings where radial reachability fails to capture feasible arc behavior.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete examples separate radial, contingent, and feasible direction systems.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C_1=\{0,1\}\) at \(0\),
\[
1\in R_{C_1}(0)\setminus T_{C_1}(0),\qquad 1\notin F_{C_1}(0).
\]
For \(C_2=\{(0,0)\}\cup\{(1/k,1/k^2):k\in\mathbb{N}\}\) at \((0,0)\),
\[
(1,0)\in T_{C_2}(0)\setminus R_{C_2}(0),\qquad (1,0)\notin F_{C_2}(0).
\]
These examples separate the radial and contingent direction systems in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two elementary sets show that radial and contingent directions are mutually incomparable and that the displayed nonzero directions need not be feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Direction-System Separation Regimes

children.title: Bouligand–Contingent Tangent Geometry
children.top_down_role: Sequential outer tangent approximation and its local geometric role.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(\bar x)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}(C-\bar x)/t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential outer tangent cone.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bouligand-contingent tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
T_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\begin{array}{l}\text{there exist }t_k\downarrow0\text{ and }v_k\to v\\\text{such that }\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\text{ for every }k\end{array}\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(T_C(\bar x)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}(C-\bar x)/t\), or \(v\in T_C(\bar x)\) exactly when \(\liminf_{t\downarrow0}d(\bar x+tv,C)/t=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The contingent cone contains directions reachable by set points along some vanishing sequence of step sizes and asymptotically matching velocities.
knowledge_statements.title: Bouligand–Contingent Tangent Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent-Cone Inverse-Image Formula under Robinson CQ
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent geometry of a smooth inverse image of a nonempty closed convex set under Robinson's constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G:X\to Y\) be continuously differentiable, let \(K\subset Y\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, define \(\Phi=G^{-1}(K)\), and let \(x_0\in\Phi\). If Robinson's constraint qualification holds at \(x_0\), then the contingent and inner tangent cones to \(\Phi\) at \(x_0\) coincide, and \[T_\Phi(x_0)=\{h\in X:DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0))\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under Robinson's constraint qualification, the contingent and inner tangent cones of a smooth inverse image of a nonempty closed convex set coincide, and the tangent cone is the derivative preimage of the target tangent cone.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\neq K\subset Y\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T^{\mathrm{cont}}_\Phi(x_0)=T^{\mathrm{inner}}_\Phi(x_0)=\{h\in X:DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0))\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Contingent Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential outer tangent cone of an arbitrary nonempty subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $x\in S$, the contingent cone is
\[
K_S(x):=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,t_i\downarrow0,\ d_i\to d\text{ such that }x+t_i d_i\in S\text{ for every }i\right\}.
\]
Its elements are called tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set S in R^n and x in S, the contingent cone consists of limits d of directions d_i such that x+t_i d_i belongs to S along a positive sequence t_i decreasing to zero. Its elements are tangent vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K_S(x)=\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists\,t_i\downarrow0,\ d_i\to d,\ x+t_i d_i\in S\ \forall i\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand and Clarke tangent cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-limit and sequential definitions for a closed subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^k\) be closed and \(x\in C\). The Bouligand tangent cone and Clarke tangent cone are
\[T_C(x):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}t^{-1}(C-x),\qquad \bar T_C(x):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\y\overset C\to x}}t^{-1}(C-y).\]
Equivalently, \(\xi\in T_C(x)\) iff there exist \(c_i\in C\) and \(t_i\downarrow0\) such that \(t_i^{-1}(c_i-x)\to\xi\). Moreover, \(\xi\in\bar T_C(x)\) iff for every \(x_i\overset C\to x\) and every \(t_i\downarrow0\), there exist \(c_i\in C\) such that \(t_i^{-1}(c_i-x_i)\to\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Bouligand tangent cone is the outer set limit of scaled displacements from x. The Clarke tangent cone is the inner set limit obtained uniformly over nearby base points in C. Sequentially, Bouligand membership requires one realizing sequence, whereas Clarke membership requires a realizing sequence for every prescribed sequence of nearby base points and positive scales tending to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C(x)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}t^{-1}(C-x),\qquad \bar T_C(x)=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\y\overset C\to x}}t^{-1}(C-y),\text{ with the stated existential and universal sequential characterizations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bouligand–Contingent Tangent Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential tangent geometry for an arbitrary nonempty subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and \(x\in S\). The Bouligand–contingent tangent cone is \[T_S(x):=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists x_k\in S,\ \exists t_k\downarrow0,\ x_k\to x,\ \frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to d\right\}.\] Its elements are the directions tangent to \(S\) at \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set S and x in S, a vector d is tangent at x when points of S approach x at positive vanishing scales and their normalized displacements converge to d. These directions form the Bouligand or contingent tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S(x)=\left\{d:\exists x_k\in S,\ \exists t_k\downarrow0,\ x_k\to x,\ (x_k-x)/t_k\to d\right\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Cone as the Polar of the Contingent Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contingent-polar normal construction for an arbitrary nonempty subset of Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $x\in S$, define
\[
N_S(x):=K_S(x)^\circ=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:z^Td\leq0\text{ for every }d\in K_S(x)\right\}.
\]
Its elements are called normal vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty set S and x in S, this normal cone is the polar of the contingent cone: it consists of vectors having nonpositive inner product with every contingent tangent direction. Its elements are normal vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_S(x)=K_S(x)^\circ=\{z\in\mathbb{R}^n:z^Td\leq0\ \forall d\in K_S(x)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and inclusion of Bouligand and Clarke tangent cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary structural comparison for tangent cones of an arbitrary closed set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(C\subset\mathbb R^k\) is closed and \(x\in C\), then \(T_C(x)\) and \(\bar T_C(x)\) are closed cones containing \(0\), and
\[\bar T_C(x)\subseteq T_C(x).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial, Contingent, Inner, and Clarke Tangent Cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal tangent constructions for a subset of a Banach space at one of its points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For $S\subseteq X$ and $x\in S$, define
$\displaystyle \mathcal R_S(x):=\{h\in X:\exists t^*>0\;\forall t\in[0,t^*],\ x+th\in S\}$,
$\displaystyle T_S(x):=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{S-x}{t}$,
$\displaystyle T_S^i(x):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{S-x}{t}$,
and
$\displaystyle T_S^c(x):=\liminf_{\substack{t\downarrow0\\S\ni x'\to x}}\frac{S-x'}{t}$,
where $S\ni x'\to x$ means that $x'$ converges to $x$ through points of $S$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a point of a set, the radial cone consists of directions whose sufficiently short line segments remain in the set; the contingent and inner tangent cones are respectively the outer and inner limits of scaled displacements; the Clarke tangent cone additionally requires the inner-limit condition uniformly over nearby base points in the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal R_S(x),\ T_S(x),\ T_S^i(x),\text{ and }T_S^c(x)\text{ are defined by the displayed radial and set-limit formulas.}

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^A(\bar x)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}(C-\bar x)/t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the fixed-base inner-limit definition of adjacent tangency.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The adjacent tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
T_C^A(\bar x):=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t}=\left\{v:\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{d(\bar x+tv,C)}{t}=0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in T_C^A(\bar x)\) when, for every sequence \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(v_k\to v\) satisfying \(\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\). Thus approximation must work along every vanishing step-size sequence, while the base point remains fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjacent direction can be approximated from the fixed base point along every sequence of vanishing step sizes.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^U(\bar x)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}(C-\bar x)/t\).

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the fixed-base convention, the Ursescu tangent cone is
\[
T_C^U(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\text{for every }t_k\downarrow0\text{ there are }v_k\to v\text{ with }\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\right\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
T_C^U(\bar x)=\liminf_{t\downarrow0}\frac{C-\bar x}{t}=\left\{v:\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{d(\bar x+tv,C)}{t}=0\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Ursescu cone consists of directions attainable asymptotically for every vanishing step-size sequence; under this convention it is the adjacent cone.

children.title: Uniform-Approach Comparison

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C^C(\bar x)\subset T_C^A(\bar x)=T_C^U(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison under the fixed-base adjacent/Ursescu convention.

source_refs.locator: A. Tangent Cones p. 196
B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
With the adjacent and Ursescu cones defined by the fixed-base inner limit,
\[
T_C^C(\bar x)\subset T_C^A(\bar x)=T_C^U(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x).
\]
Each inclusion can be strict for a closed nonconvex set. If \(C\) is convex, then
\[
T_C^C(\bar x)=T_C^A(\bar x)=T_C^U(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\{\lambda(y-\bar x):\lambda\ge0,\ y\in C\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clarke tangency lies inside the coincident fixed-base adjacent and Ursescu cones, which lie inside contingent tangency; convex sets eliminate these differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Approach Comparison

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Clarke tangent cone to \(C\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
T_C^C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb{R}^n:\lim_{\substack{x\to_C\bar x\\t\downarrow0}}\frac{d(x+tv,C)}{t}=0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, for every \(x_k\to_C\bar x\) and every \(t_k\downarrow0\), there exist \(v_k\to v\) such that \(x_k+t_kv_k\in C\). The set \(T_C^C(\bar x)\) is a closed convex cone contained in \(T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Clarke tangent direction remains asymptotically feasible for every nearby base point and every vanishing step-size sequence; the resulting cone is closed and convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relation between Clarke and contingent tangent cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of the Clarke tangent cone with the contingent cone, including the convex-set equality case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is nonempty and $x\in S$, then
\[
T_S(x)\subseteq K_S(x).
\]
If, in addition, $S$ is convex, then
\[
T_S(x)=K_S(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every nonempty set, the Clarke tangent cone is contained in the contingent cone. If the set is convex, the two cones coincide.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S(x)\subseteq K_S(x),\qquad S\text{ convex}\implies T_S(x)=K_S(x)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records the metric property ensuring that the distance function admits Clarke derivatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential characterization of the Clarke tangent cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal-sequence characterization of Clarke tangent directions for an arbitrary nonempty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty set $S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $x\in S$,
\[
T_S(x)=\left\{d\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \middle|\ \begin{array}{l}
\text{for every }t_i\downarrow0\text{ and every }x_i\to x\text{ with }x_i\in S,\\
\text{there exist }d_i\to d\text{ such that }x_i+t_i d_i\in S
\end{array}\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction d is Clarke tangent at x exactly when, for every positive sequence decreasing to zero and every sequence of points in S converging to x, d can be approximated by directions whose corresponding perturbations remain in S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d\in T_S(x)\iff\forall(t_i\downarrow0)\ \forall(x_i\in S,\ x_i\to x)\ \exists(d_i\to d):\ x_i+t_i d_i\in S

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke tangent cone as a lower limit of scaled set differences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the Clarke tangent cone through the lower limit of nearby scaled displacement sets; the limit variable in the extract is interpreted as \(\alpha\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega\). For \(x'\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha>0\), define
\[
A(x',\alpha)=\frac{1}{\alpha}(\Omega-x').
\]
Then
\[
T(x,\Omega)=\liminf_{\substack{x'\to x\\ \alpha\downarrow0}}A(x',\alpha).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke tangent cone is the lower limit, as the base point approaches the reference point and the positive scale tends to zero, of the scaled displacement sets from the base point to the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T(x,\Omega)=\liminf_{x'\to x,\,\alpha\downarrow0}A(x',\alpha)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Uniform and sequential characterizations of Clarke tangent directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets the evident occurrence of \(T(x,g)\) as \(T(x,\Omega)\) and makes explicit the standard restriction of nearby base points to \(\Omega\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(x\in\operatorname{cl}\Omega\), and \(g\in\mathbb R^n\). The following are equivalent:
\[
\text{(i) }g\in T(x,\Omega);
\]
\[
\text{(ii) }\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists\delta>0\;\forall x'\in\Omega\cap\mathcal B_\delta(x)\;\forall\alpha\in(0,\delta)\;\exists g'\in\mathcal B_\varepsilon(g):\ x'+\alpha g'\in\Omega;
\]
\[
\text{(iii) whenever }x_k'\in\Omega,	x_k'\to x,	\alpha_k\downarrow0,	\text{there exist }g_k\to g\text{ with }x_k'+\alpha_k g_k\in\Omega.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is Clarke tangent exactly when every sufficiently nearby feasible base point and sufficiently small positive step admits a nearby direction remaining feasible. Equivalently, this property holds along every convergent sequence of feasible base points and every positive step-size sequence decreasing to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{(i)}\iff\text{(ii)}\iff\text{(iii)}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Nearby-Point Representation of the Clarke Tangent Cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space inclusions for Clarke tangent cones and the stronger nearby-point representation available in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $S$ be a closed, not necessarily convex, subset of a Banach space $X$, and let $x\in S$. Then $T_S^c(x)$ is convex,
\[
T_S^c(x)\subseteq T_S^i(x),
\qquad
T_S^c(x)\subseteq\liminf_{S\ni x'\to x}T_S(x').
\]
If $X$ is finite dimensional, then
\[
T_S^c(x)=\liminf_{S\ni x'\to x}T_S(x').
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed set in a Banach space, the Clarke tangent cone is convex, is contained in the inner tangent cone, and is contained in the lower limit of nearby contingent cones. In finite-dimensional spaces, the latter inclusion is an equality.
assumptions_latex: $S\subseteq X$ is closed and need not be convex.
The equality with the lower limit of nearby contingent cones additionally assumes $\dim X<\infty$.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S^c(x)\text{ is convex},\quad T_S^c(x)\subseteq T_S^i(x),\quad T_S^c(x)\subseteq\liminf_{S\ni x'\to x}T_S(x'),\quad \dim X<\infty\Rightarrow T_S^c(x)=\liminf_{S\ni x'\to x}T_S(x').

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivable Tangent Vector by Small-Step Approximation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines tangency for an arbitrary Euclidean subset and records positive homogeneity and the convex feasible-direction inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n and x\in Q. A vector s\in\mathbb R^n is tangent to Q at x if, for every sufficiently small \tau>0, there exists x(\tau)\in Q such that \|x(\tau)-(x+\tau s)\|=o(\tau) as \tau\downarrow0. The set S_Q(x) of such vectors is a cone. If Q is convex, every feasible direction is tangent, but the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is tangent when, at every sufficiently small positive step, a point of the set approximates the corresponding ray with error negligible relative to the step. These vectors form a cone. For convex sets, every feasible direction is tangent, although a tangent direction need not be feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_Q(x)=\left\{s:\forall\text{ sufficiently small }\tau>0\ \exists x(\tau)\in Q,\ \|x(\tau)-(x+\tau s)\|=o(\tau)\right\},\qquad s\in S_Q(x),\ \lambda\geq0\Rightarrow\lambda s\in S_Q(x).

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone at a nearby point

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects a directional outer limit of nearby Bouligand cones; conventions vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a selected approach direction \(d\in T_C(\bar x)\), define the directionally localized tangent cone by
\[
T_C(\bar x;d):=\limsup_{\substack{t\downarrow0,\ d'\to d\\\bar x+td'\in C}}T_C(\bar x+td').
\]
Thus \(w\in T_C(\bar x;d)\) exactly when there exist \(t_k\downarrow0\), \(d_k\to d\), and \(w_k\to w\) such that \(x_k:=\bar x+t_kd_k\in C\) and \(w_k\in T_C(x_k)\) for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A directional tangent cone collects limiting tangent directions at points approaching the reference point specifically along a selected first-order direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Upper and Lower Limits of Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-based set limits for a parameterized family of subsets of a Banach space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $X$ be a Banach space and let $(A_t)$ be a family of subsets of $X$. Define
$\displaystyle \limsup_{t\to t_0}A_t:=\{x\in X:\liminf_{t\to t_0}\operatorname{dist}(x,A_t)=0\}$
and
$\displaystyle \liminf_{t\to t_0}A_t:=\{x\in X:\limsup_{t\to t_0}\operatorname{dist}(x,A_t)=0\}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The upper set limit consists of points whose distance to the varying sets has lower limit zero; the lower set limit consists of points whose distance has upper limit zero.
assumptions_latex: A_t\subseteq X$ is a parameterized family of sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \limsup_{t\to t_0}A_t=\{x:\liminf_{t\to t_0}\operatorname{dist}(x,A_t)=0\},\quad \liminf_{t\to t_0}A_t=\{x:\limsup_{t\to t_0}\operatorname{dist}(x,A_t)=0\}.

notation.meaning: tangent cone to C relative to the ambient set Q

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses intersection localization as the relative-tangent convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Bouligand tangent cone to \(C\) relative to an ambient or active set \(Q\) at \(\bar x\) is
\[
T_{C\mid Q}(\bar x):=T_{C\cap Q}(\bar x)=\limsup_{t\downarrow0}\frac{(C\cap Q)-\bar x}{t}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in T_{C\mid Q}(\bar x)\) when there are \(t_k\downarrow0\) and \(v_k\to v\) with \(\bar x+t_kv_k\in C\cap Q\). Always \(T_{C\mid Q}(\bar x)\subset T_C(\bar x)\cap T_Q(\bar x)\); equality requires additional intersection regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative tangency restricts approximating points to both the set and a chosen ambient or active set; it is generally smaller than intersecting tangent cones.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(g_i(x)\le 0\) and \(h_j(x)=0\), let \(\bar x\) be feasible and let \(L_C(\bar x)\) be the linearized cone. The critical cone is
\[

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Critical cone and its linearized-optimality interpretation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition for the constrained problem, including the stated linearized-problem characterization and its failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The critical cone of \((P)\) at \(x_0\) is
\[
C(x_0):=\{h\in T_Q(x_0):DG(x_0)h\in T_K(G(x_0)),\ Df(x_0)h\leq 0\}.
\]
Moreover, \(h=0\) is an optimal solution of the linearized problem if and only if \(Df(x_0)h=0\) for every \(h\in C(x_0)\). In that case, \(C(x_0)\) is the set of optimal solutions of the linearized problem. The definition remains meaningful when zero is not an optimal solution of that problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The critical cone contains the tangent directions satisfying the linearized constraints and having nonpositive objective derivative. Zero solves the linearized problem exactly when the objective derivative vanishes on this cone; then the cone is the linearized solution set. The definition still applies when zero is not linearly optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any differentiable constraint representation, feasible-arc velocities satisfy \(T_C(\bar x)\subseteq L_C(\bar x)\), but equality can fail without an appropriate constraint qualification. Consider
\[
C=\{x\in\mathbb R:x^2\le 0\}=\{0\},\qquad \bar x=0.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is geometrically derivable at \(\bar x\in C\) if, for every \(v\in T_C(\bar x)\), there exist \(\varepsilon>0\) and an arc \(\gamma:[0,\varepsilon)\to C\) such that
\[
\gamma(0)=\bar x,\qquad \lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac{\gamma(t)-\bar x}{t}=v.
\]
Equivalently, every direction admitted by the sequential contingent construction is realized as the right derivative of a single feasible arc. The property is local at \(\bar x\); a set is geometrically derivable when it has this property at each of its points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is geometrically derivable when every contingent direction is realized by the initial velocity of one feasible arc.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Outer- and Inner-Limit Characterization of Tangency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit representations of sequential and derivable tangents to an arbitrary Euclidean set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\). The tangent cone is the closed cone \[T_C(\bar x)=\limsup_{\tau\searrow0}\tau^{-1}(C-\bar x).\] The derivable tangent vectors form the corresponding closed inner-limit cone \[\liminf_{\tau\searrow0}\tau^{-1}(C-\bar x).\] Consequently, \(C\) is geometrically derivable at \(\bar x\) iff \(\tau^{-1}(C-\bar x)\) converges as \(\tau\searrow0\), in which case its full limit equals \(T_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At any point of a Euclidean set, the tangent vectors form a closed cone equal to the outer limit of the rescaled translated sets. The derivable tangent vectors form the corresponding closed inner-limit cone. The set is geometrically derivable at the point exactly when these rescaled sets have a full limit, which then equals the tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C(\bar x)=\limsup_{\tau\searrow0}\tau^{-1}(C-\bar x)\text{ is a closed cone},\quad T_C^{\mathrm{der}}(\bar x)=\liminf_{\tau\searrow0}\tau^{-1}(C-\bar x)\text{ is a closed cone},\quad C\text{ is geometrically derivable at }\bar x\iff\lim_{\tau\searrow0}\tau^{-1}(C-\bar x)=T_C(\bar x).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
C=(\mathbb R\times\{0\})\cup(\{0\}\times\mathbb R),\qquad \bar x=(0,0).
\]
Every direction lying on either coordinate axis is radial and is available at every positive scale, so
\[
R_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)=T_C^A(\bar x)=C.
\]
However, a nonzero axial direction cannot remain tangent when the base point approaches \(\bar x\) along the other axis. Consequently the robust Clarke tangent cone is \(T_C^C(\bar x)=\{0\}\). Thus contingent, adjacent, and radial tangency can agree while differing strictly from Clarke tangency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At the crossing of two axes, ordinary sequential and radial tangents contain both axes, whereas the robust Clarke tangent contains only zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangential Jacobian, divergence, and strain operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects the first-order intrinsic operators and their principal ambient-extension identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the smooth tubular-neighborhood assumptions, let \(v\in C^1(\Gamma)^M\), \(M\ge1\), and let \(V\) extend \(v\). Define
\[
D_\Gamma v:=\left.D(v\circ p)\right|_\Gamma,
\qquad (D_\Gamma v)_{ij}=(\nabla_\Gamma v_i)_j.
\]
Then
\[
D_\Gamma v=\left.DV\right|_\Gamma-\left.(DVn)n^*\right|_\Gamma
=\left.(DVP)\right|_\Gamma,
\]
\[
D(v\circ p)=(D_\Gamma v)\circ p\,[I-bD^2b],
\qquad D(v\circ p)\nabla b=0.
\]
For \(v\in C^1(\Gamma)^N\), define
\[
\operatorname{div}_\Gamma v:=\left.\operatorname{div}(v\circ p)\right|_\Gamma
=\operatorname{tr}(D_\Gamma v)
=\left.\operatorname{div}V\right|_\Gamma-(DVn)\cdot n,
\]
and
\[
\varepsilon_\Gamma(v):=\tfrac12(D_\Gamma v+D_\Gamma v^*),
\qquad \varepsilon_\Gamma(v)=\left.\varepsilon(v\circ p)\right|_\Gamma.
\]
Furthermore,
\[
D_\Gamma n=\left.D^2b\right|_\Gamma= D_\Gamma n^*,
\qquad \varepsilon_\Gamma(n)=\left.D^2b\right|_\Gamma,
\]
and for a matrix or tensor field \(A\),
\[
(\operatorname{div}_\Gamma A)_i:=\operatorname{div}_\Gamma(A_{i,\cdot}).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The tangential Jacobian is the Jacobian of the nearest-point extension restricted to the surface, equivalently the ambient extension Jacobian projected away from the normal direction. Its trace defines tangential divergence, its symmetric part defines tangential strain, and the normal field has tangential Jacobian equal to the boundary Hessian of the signed-distance function. Tensor divergence is defined row by row.

v\in C^1(\Gamma)^N\text{ when }\operatorname{div}_\Gamma v\text{ is used}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a nonempty closed convex set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), its convex normal cone is
\[
N_C(\bar x):=\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }x\in C\}.
\]
If the negative polar of a cone \(K\) is \(K^\circ:=\{v:\langle v,d\rangle\le0\ \text{for every }d\in K\}\), then
\[
N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ.
\]
Thus global supporting inequalities and the polar of local feasible directions define the same normal geometry for convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set, normal vectors globally support the set at the point, and the normal cone is the tangent cone's negative polar.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Normal Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal Map and Normal Equation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Projection-based equation representation associated with a variational inequality on a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty, closed, and convex and let F:C\to\mathbb{R}^n. The normal map associated with (F,C) is F_C:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n defined by F_C(z)=F(\Pi_C(z))+z-\Pi_C(z). The equation F_C(z)=0 is the normal equation. In addition, \Pi_C(z) is the unique \bar z\in C such that z-\bar z\in\mathcal N(\bar z;C).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal map adds the projection residual to F evaluated at the projected point, and its zero equation is the normal equation. Projection onto C is equivalently characterized by the displacement from the projection lying in the normal cone at the projected point.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), the regular, or Fréchet, normal cone is
\[
\widehat N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v\in\mathbb R^n:\limsup_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\in C,\ x\ne\bar x}}\frac{\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle}{\|x-\bar x\|}\le0\right\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(v\in\widehat N_C(\bar x)\) precisely when
\[
\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le o(\|x-\bar x\|)\quad\text{as }x\to\bar x\text{ within }C.
\]
This cone records vectors that support the set to first order at the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular normal has nonpositive inner product with nearby feasible displacements up to an error negligible relative to the displacement length.
knowledge_statements.title: Regular–Fréchet Normal Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient characterization of regular normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes regular normals by gradients of smooth functions maximized relative to the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subset\mathbb{R}^n and \bar{x}\in C. Then v\in\widehat N_C(\bar{x}) if and only if there exists a function h that has a local maximum relative to C at \bar{x}, is differentiable at \bar{x}, and satisfies \nabla h(\bar{x})=v. Moreover, h may be chosen in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n) so that \bar{x} is its unique global maximizer relative to C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is a regular normal to a set at a point exactly when it is the gradient there of a differentiable function having a relative local maximum at that point. The function can be chosen smooth with that point as its unique relative global maximizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v\in\widehat N_C(\bar{x})\iff\exists h:\ \bar{x}\text{ is a local maximizer of }h\text{ on }C,\ h\text{ is differentiable at }\bar{x},\ \nabla h(\bar{x})=v;\text{ moreover }h\in C^\infty\text{ may have }\bar{x}\text{ as its unique global maximizer on }C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hemi-Lipschitzian, strictly hemi-Lipschitzian, and hemismooth sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph-preimage definitions for subsets of Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset Z\), \(\bar z\in\Omega\), and let \(\mathcal B\) denote a differentiability concept. The set \(\Omega\) is hemi-Lipschitzian around \(\bar z\) if there exist Banach spaces \(X,Y\), mappings \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Z\to X\times Y\), and neighborhoods \(U\) of \(\bar z\) and \(V\) of \(g(\bar z)\), such that \(g(\bar z)=(\bar x,f(\bar x))\), \(g\) is strictly Fréchet differentiable at \(\bar z\) with surjective derivative, \(f\) is Lipschitz continuous around \(\bar x\), and \(\Omega\cap U=g^{-1}(V\cap\operatorname{gph}f)\). It is strictly hemi-Lipschitzian at \(\bar z\) if \(f\) is additionally weak-star strictly Lipschitzian at \(\bar x\). It is \(\mathcal B\)-hemismooth at \(\bar z\) if it is hemi-Lipschitzian and \(f\) can be chosen \(\mathcal B\)-differentiable at \(\bar x\). When \(\nabla g(\bar z)\) is invertible, the representation gives the corresponding Lipschitzian-set regime; imposing both invertibility and \(\mathcal B\)-differentiability gives the analogous \(\mathcal B\)-smooth-set notion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is hemi-Lipschitzian when it is locally the preimage, under a strictly Fréchet differentiable mapping with surjective derivative, of the graph of a locally Lipschitz mapping. Weak-star strict Lipschitz continuity of the graphing map gives strict hemi-Lipschitzianity, and a chosen differentiability property gives hemismoothness. Invertibility of the representing derivative yields the corresponding Lipschitzian or smooth-set regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Omega\text{ is hemi-Lipschitzian, strictly hemi-Lipschitzian, or }\mathcal B\text{-hemismooth according to the stated graph-preimage conditions}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexified-normal linearity and a characterization of normal regularity under an Asplund representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Omega\subset Z\) be strictly hemi-Lipschitzian at \(\bar z\), and suppose the representation space \(X\) in the definition can be chosen Asplund. Then the convexified normal cone to \(\Omega\) at \(\bar z\) is a linear subspace of \(Z^*\). In particular, when \(\Omega\) is locally closed around \(\bar z\) and \(Z\) is Asplund, the Clarke normal cone is a linear subspace. Moreover, \(\Omega\) is normally regular at \(\bar z\) if and only if it is simultaneously \(w\mathcal F\)-smooth and strictly \(w\mathcal H\)-smooth at \(\bar z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly hemi-Lipschitzian set whose representation space can be chosen Asplund, the convexified normal cone is a linear subspace. Under local closedness and an Asplund ambient space, this applies to the Clarke normal cone. Normal regularity is equivalent to simultaneous weak Fréchet smoothness and strict weak Hadamard smoothness.

X\text{ in its representation can be chosen Asplund}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a locally closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), a vector \(v\) is proximal normal at \(\bar x\) when there exists \(r>0\) such that \(\bar x\in P_C(\bar x+rv)\). Equivalently, after rescaling the parameter, there exist \(\sigma\ge0\) and a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) satisfying
\[
\langle v,x-\bar x\rangle\le\frac{\sigma}{2}\|x-\bar x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }x\in C\cap U.
\]
The collection of all such vectors is the proximal normal cone \(N_C^P(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal points from a nearest feasible point toward an exterior center and equivalently provides local quadratic support.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines proximal normals by quadratic support and gives their nearest-point characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^k\) be closed and \(\bar x\in C\). Then \[N_C^P(\bar x):=\{\eta\in\mathbb R^k:\exists M\ge0\text{ such that }\eta\cdot(x-\bar x)\le M\lVert x-\bar x\rVert^2\ \forall x\in C\}.\] Equivalently, \(\eta\in N_C^P(\bar x)\) if and only if there exist \(y\in\mathbb R^k\) and \(\alpha\ge0\) such that \(\bar x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{z\in C}\lVert y-z\rVert\) and \(\eta=\alpha(y-\bar x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Approximation of horizontal proximal epigraph normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonzero horizontal proximal normal to an epigraph is approximated by proximal normals with small strictly negative vertical components at nearby graph points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nearest-point characterization of proximal normals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of every proximal normal; the exterior-point interpretation requires a nonzero normal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $C\subset\mathbb R^k$ be closed, $x\in C$, and $p\in\mathbb R^k$. Then
\[
p\in N_C^P(x)
\iff
\exists z\in\mathbb R^k,\ r>0:\quad
\lVert z-x\rVert=\min_{y\in C}\lVert z-y\rVert,
\quad p=r(z-x).
\]
If $p\ne0$, then $z\notin C$, $x$ is a closest point of $C$ to $z$, and $p$ has the direction $z-x$. Membership in proximal normal cones is not generally preserved under limits with varying base points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector is proximal normal exactly when it is a positive multiple of the displacement from a nearest point of the set to an ambient point. For a nonzero normal that point is outside the set. Proximal-normal membership can fail to persist as the base point varies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\in N_C^P(x)\iff \exists z\in\mathbb R^k,\ r>0:\ x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in C}\lVert z-y\rVert\ \text{and}\ p=r(z-x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proximal normal cone and nearest-point representation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean proximal normals to a closed set, including the equivalent distance and projection formulations stated in the extract.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a closed set $C\subset\mathbb R^k$ and $x\in C$,
\[
N_C^P(x):=\left\{p\in\mathbb R^k:\exists M>0\ \forall y\in C,\ p\cdot(y-x)\le M\lVert y-x\rVert^2\right\}.
\]
For such $M$, setting $z=x+(2M)^{-1}p$ gives
\[
\lVert z-y\rVert\ge (2M)^{-1}\lVert p\rVert=\lVert z-x\rVert\qquad\forall y\in C.
\]
Equivalently, there exist $z\in\mathbb R^k$ and $r>0$ such that
\[
\lVert z-x\rVert=\min_{y\in C}\lVert z-y\rVert,
\qquad p=r(z-x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal normal satisfies a quadratic supporting inequality. Equivalently, it is a positive multiple of the displacement from a nearest point of the set to a suitable ambient point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p\in N_C^P(x)\iff \exists M>0\ \forall y\in C,\ p\cdot(y-x)\le M\lVert y-x\rVert^2,\text{ with the stated equivalent distance and nearest-point representations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a locally closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), the limiting, or Mordukhovich, normal cone is
\[
N_C(\bar x):=\left\{v:\exists x_k\to\bar x,\ x_k\in C,\ \exists v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\right\}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
N_C(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{\substack{x\to\bar x\\x\in C}}\widehat N_C(x).
\]
Unlike the regular normal cone, \(N_C(\bar x)\) need not be convex; it preserves normals arising from distinct nearby geometric branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting normal is the limit of regular normals taken at feasible points approaching the reference point.

If \(\bar x\in\partial C\), it contains a nonzero vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a locally closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in C\), the Clarke normal cone is the negative polar of the Clarke tangent cone:
\[
N_C^C(\bar x):=T_C^C(\bar x)^\circ.
\]
In finite dimensions it is also the closed convex hull of the limiting normal cone:
\[
N_C^C(\bar x)=\operatorname{cl}\operatorname{co}N_C(\bar x).
\]
Consequently \(N_C^C(\bar x)\) is always a closed convex cone and combines limiting normals contributed by different nearby branches of the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke normal is the polar of the robust Clarke tangent and, in finite dimensions, the closed convex hull of limiting normals.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a locally closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\), a point \(\bar x\in C\), and a direction \(d\in\mathbb R^n\), the directional limiting normal cone is
\[
N_C(\bar x;d):=\left\{v:\begin{array}{l}\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ d_k\to d,\ \bar x+t_kd_k\in C,\\[2pt]\exists v_k\to v\ \text{with }v_k\in\widehat N_C(\bar x+t_kd_k)\end{array}\right\}.
\]
It is empty when \(d\notin T_C(\bar x)\), and every directional limiting normal is an ordinary limiting normal, so \(N_C(\bar x;d)\subseteq N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional limiting normals arise from regular normals along feasible points approaching the reference point with a prescribed first-order direction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(\mathbb R^n\), bounded sequences have norm-convergent subsequences and the dual space is canonically \(\mathbb R^n\). Hence, if \(x_k\to\bar x\), \(v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\), and \((v_k)\) is bounded, some subsequence converges in norm to a vector \(v\). Every such limit belongs to \(N_C(\bar x)\). A vector \(v\) is proximal normal to \(C\) at \(x\) precisely when there exists \(r>0\) such that \(x\in P_C(x+rv)\). Equivalently, for some \(r>0\),
\[\langle v,z-x\rangle\leq \frac{1}{2r}\|z-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.\]
Thus the inner product converts a nearest-point relation into a quadratic supporting inequality. The zero vector satisfies the characterization trivially.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a Hilbert space, proximal normals are exactly directions from a point toward an external point that projects back to it.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential weak-star realization of limiting normals in an Asplund space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in C\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\), define
\[\widehat N_{C,\varepsilon}(x):=\left\{x^*\in X^*: \limsup_{\substack{u\to x\\u\in C,\,u\ne x}}\frac{\langle x^*,u-x\rangle}{\|u-x\|}\leq\varepsilon\right\}.\]
The limiting normal cone in the Asplund regime is represented by all \(x^*\in X^*\) for which sequences \(x_k\to_C\bar x\), \(\varepsilon_k\downarrow0\), and \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_{C,\varepsilon_k}(x_k)\) exist with \(x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}x^*\). This sequential representation is the normal construction used by Asplund-space calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Limiting normals in an Asplund space arise as weak-star limits of approximate Fréchet normals at nearby feasible points.
knowledge_statements.title: Asplund-Space Normal Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(C\) is sequentially normally compact at \(\bar x\) if, for every sequence \(x_k\in C\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\) and every sequence \(x_k^*\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\), the implication
\[x_k^*\xrightarrow{w^*}0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\|x_k^*\|\to0\]
holds. The condition excludes nonvanishing Fréchet normals that disappear only in the weak-star topology and supplies the compactness needed in limiting-normal calculus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential normal compactness prevents nearby nonzero regular normals from converging weak-star, but not strongly, to zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normals to generalized epigraphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For \(\mathcal E(f,\Omega,\Theta)=\{(x,z):x\in\Omega,\ f(x)-z\in\Theta\}\) in Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to Z\), \(\bar x\in\Omega\), and \(f(\bar x)-\bar z\in\Theta\). (i) If \(f\) is locally Lipschitz near \(\bar x\) relative to \(\Omega\), then \(D_M^*f_\Omega(\bar x)(z^*)=\partial\langle z^*,f_\Omega\rangle(\bar x)\) for every \(z^*\in Z^*\). (ii) Always, \((x^*,z^*)\in N((\bar x,\bar z);\mathcal E(f,\Omega,\Theta))\) implies \(-z^*\in N(f(\bar x)-\bar z;\Theta)\). If \(X,Z\) are Asplund, \(f\) is relatively continuous near \(\bar x\), and \(\Omega,\Theta\) are locally closed at the reference points, then every such normal also satisfies \(x^*\in D_N^*f_\Omega(\bar x)(z^*)\). (iii) If additionally \(f\) is relatively locally Lipschitz and \(f_\Omega\) is strongly coderivatively normal at \(\bar x\), then every generalized-epigraph normal satisfies \(x^*\in\partial\langle z^*,f_\Omega\rangle(\bar x)\) and \(-z^*\in N(f(\bar x)-\bar z;\Theta)\). (iv) Relative local Lipschitz continuity gives the reverse inclusion in the scalarized-subdifferential representation in arbitrary Banach spaces; under strong coderivative normality it also gives the reverse inclusion in the normal-coderivative representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second component of every normal to a generalized epigraph is a negative normal to the ordering set. Under Asplund and closedness hypotheses, the first component is described by a normal coderivative; local Lipschitz continuity and strong coderivative normality yield exact scalarized-subdifferential and coderivative representations.
assumptions_latex: \text{Relative Lipschitz continuity, Asplundness, local closedness, and strong coderivative normality are imposed in the indicated branches.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N((\bar x,\bar z);\mathcal E(f,\Omega,\Theta))\subset\{(x^*,z^*):x^*\in D_N^*f_\Omega(\bar x)(z^*),\ -z^*\in N(f(\bar x)-\bar z;\Theta)\},\text{ with the stated reverse inclusions and scalarized representation under stronger assumptions.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sufficient conditions for weak-star extensibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complementation and weak-star sequential compactness criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a closed linear subspace of a Banach space \(X\). Then \(V\) is weak-star extensible in \(X\) if either (a) \(V\) is complemented in \(X\), so that \(X=V\oplus L\) for some closed linear subspace \(L\subset X\), or (b) the closed unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak-star sequentially compact. Condition (b) holds, in particular, when \(X\) is Asplund or weakly compactly generated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed subspace is weak-star extensible if it is complemented in the ambient Banach space, or if the ambient dual unit ball is weak-star sequentially compact; the latter includes Asplund and weakly compactly generated spaces.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal cone of a closed convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition in a Banach space, including the off-set boundary case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subset W\) be nonempty, closed, and convex, where \(W\) is a Banach space. For \(w\in W\), define
\[
N_S(w)=\begin{cases}
\{y\in W^*: \langle y,z-w\rangle_{W^*,W}\le 0\ \forall z\in S\},&w\in S,\\
\varnothing,&w\notin S.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(N_S:W\rightrightarrows W^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex subset S of a Banach space W, the normal cone at a point w in S consists of all continuous linear functionals whose pairing with every feasible displacement z−w is nonpositive; it is empty when w is outside S.
assumptions_latex: \varnothing\ne S\subset W\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_S(w)=\begin{cases}\{y\in W^*: \langle y,z-w\rangle\le0\ \forall z\in S\},&w\in S,\\\varnothing,&w\notin S.\end{cases}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential and topological normal structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines both limiting constructions generated by an arbitrary prenormal structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat{\mathcal N}\) be a prenormal structure on a Banach space \(X\). knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coderivatively Normal and Strongly Coderivatively Normal Mappings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise definitions for set-valued mappings between Banach spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let F:X\rightrightarrows Y be a set-valued mapping between Banach spaces and let (\bar x,\bar y)\in\operatorname{gph}F. The mapping F is coderivatively normal at (\bar x,\bar y) if \|D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|=\|D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|. It is strongly coderivatively normal there if D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y), and this common mapping is denoted D^*F(\bar x,\bar y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a graph point, coderivative normality means that the mixed and normal coderivatives have equal norms. Strong coderivative normality means that the two coderivative mappings themselves coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|=\|D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)\|,\quad\text{or strongly }D_M^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=D_N^*F(\bar x,\bar y)=:D^*F(\bar x,\bar y).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal cone as the polar of the tangent cone
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent–normal polarity in a normed space, including closedness and the interior-point case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, \(S\subset X\), and \(x\in S\). For \(A\subset X\), define \(A^{\Delta}:=\{\zeta\in X^*: \langle\zeta,a\rangle\le 0\ \forall a\in A\}\). Then \(N_S(x):=T_S(x)^{\Delta}=\{\zeta\in X^*: \langle\zeta,v\rangle\le 0\ \forall v\in T_S(x)\}\). Moreover, \(N_S(x)\) is a closed cone in \(X^*\), and \(x\in\operatorname{int}S\) implies \(T_S(x)=X\) and \(N_S(x)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal cone is the polar of the tangent cone and is closed in the dual space. At an interior point, the tangent cone is the whole space and the normal cone is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_S(x)=T_S(x)^{\Delta},\quad N_S(x)\text{ is a closed cone},\quad x\in\operatorname{int}S\Rightarrow T_S(x)=X\text{ and }N_S(x)=\{0\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Clarke tangent and normal cones
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-function definition of the Clarke tangent cone and definition of the Clarke normal cone by polarity, with locality and interior-point properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in S\), define \(T_S^C(x)=\{v\in X:d_S^{\circ}(x;v)=0\}\) and \(N_S^C(x)=(T_S^C(x))^{\Delta}=\{\zeta\in X^*:\langle\zeta,v\rangle\le 0\ \forall v\in T_S^C(x)\}\). Since \(d_S^{\circ}(x;v)\ge 0\), the condition defining \(T_S^C(x)\) may equivalently be written \(d_S^{\circ}(x;v)\le 0\). Both sets are cones. If \(x\in\operatorname{int}S\), then \(T_S^C(x)=X\) and \(N_S^C(x)=\{0\}\); sets agreeing in a neighborhood of \(x\) have the same Clarke tangent and normal cones there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Clarke tangent cone consists of directions in which the Clarke directional derivative of the distance to S is zero, and the Clarke normal cone is its polar. The construction is local, and an interior point has the whole space as its tangent cone and only the zero normal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S^C(x)=\{v\in X:d_S^{\circ}(x;v)=0\}=\{v\in X:d_S^{\circ}(x;v)\le 0\},\qquad N_S^C(x)=(T_S^C(x))^{\Delta}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The contingent tangent cone is
\[T_C(x):=\left\{h:\exists t_k\downarrow0,\ \exists x_k\in C,\ x_k\to x,\ \frac{x_k-x}{t_k}\to h\right\}.\]
The Fréchet normal cone satisfies the exact local polarity formula
\[\widehat N_C(x)=T_C(x)^\circ=\{x^*\in X^*: \langle x^*,h\rangle\leq0\ \forall h\in T_C(x)\}.\]
This equality concerns regular normals at the fixed point; it does not assert that the generally nonconvex limiting normal cone is the polar of \(T_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional normed space, regular normals at a point are exactly the covectors nonpositive on every contingent tangent direction there.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A set \(S\) is regular at \(x\in S\) when \(T_S(x)=T_S^C(x)\). In this case, polarity yields \(N_S^C(x)=(T_S^C(x))^{\Delta}=(T_S(x))^{\Delta}=N_S(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set is regular at a point when its tangent cone equals its Clarke tangent cone. At such a point, the corresponding normal and Clarke normal cones also agree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is regular at }x\iff T_S(x)=T_S^C(x),\qquad S\text{ regular at }x\Rightarrow N_S^C(x)=N_S(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent and Normal Spaces of a Regular Equality Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the tangent and normal geometry of a continuously differentiable equality set under surjectivity of its derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\to Y\) be continuously differentiable in a neighborhood of \(x\), let \(S=\{u\in X:F(u)=0\}\), suppose \(x\in S\), and assume \(F'(x):X\to Y\) is surjective. Then
\[T_S(x)=T_S^C(x)=\{v\in X:F'(x)v=0\},\]
\[N_S(x)=N_S^C(x)=\{\Lambda\circ F'(x)\in X^*:\Lambda\in Y^*\}=F'(x)^*Y^*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable equality set at a point where the derivative is surjective, the ordinary and Clarke tangent cones equal the derivative's kernel, while the ordinary and Clarke normal cones equal the range of its adjoint.
assumptions_latex: F:X\to Y\text{ is continuously differentiable near }x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_S(x)=T_S^C(x)=\ker F'(x),\qquad N_S(x)=N_S^C(x)=F'(x)^*Y^*.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangent and Normal Cones of a Closed Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Establishes regularity and explicit tangent- and normal-cone formulas for a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subset X\) be closed and convex and let \(x\in S\). Then \(S\) is regular at \(x\), and
\[T_S^C(x)=T_S(x)=\operatorname{cl}\left\{\frac{u-x}{t}:u\in S,\ t>0\right\},\]
\[N_S^C(x)=N_S(x)=\left\{\zeta\in X^*:\langle\zeta,u-x\rangle\le 0\ \text{for all }u\in S\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every closed convex set is regular at each of its points. Its tangent cone is the closure of the cone of feasible chords, and its normal cone consists of the continuous linear functionals nonpositive on every feasible displacement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S\text{ is regular at }x,\quad T_S^C(x)=T_S(x)=\operatorname{cl}\left\{\frac{u-x}{t}:u\in S,\ t>0\right\},\quad N_S^C(x)=N_S(x)=\left\{\zeta\in X^*:\langle\zeta,u-x\rangle\le0\ \forall u\in S\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangents and normals to finite intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes unconditional inclusions, the normal qualification, and the stronger regular-set equalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=\bigcap_{i=1}^mC_i for closed C_i\subset\mathbb R^n and let \bar x\in C. Unconditionally, T_C(\bar x)\subset\bigcap_iT_{C_i}(\bar x) and \widehat N_C(\bar x)\supset\sum_i\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x). If v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x) and \sum_i v_i=0 imply v_i=0 for every i, then \widehat T_C(\bar x)\supset\bigcap_i\widehat T_{C_i}(\bar x) and N_C(\bar x)\subset\sum_iN_{C_i}(\bar x). If, additionally, every C_i is regular at \bar x, then C is regular there and T_C(\bar x)=\bigcap_iT_{C_i}(\bar x), N_C(\bar x)=\sum_iN_{C_i}(\bar x). For m=2, the qualification holds when C_1,C_2 are convex and cannot be separated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite intersection of closed sets, contingent tangents are always contained in the intersection of the individual tangents, while regular normals contain their sum. A noncancellation condition on limiting normals yields the reverse regular-tangent inclusion and an upper estimate for limiting normals. If every set is regular, the intersection is regular and both rules become equalities. For two convex sets, nonseparability suffices for the qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_C(\bar x)\subset\bigcap_iT_{C_i}(\bar x),\quad \widehat N_C(\bar x)\supset\sum_i\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x);\quad [\sum_i v_i=0,\ v_i\in N_{C_i}(\bar x)\Rightarrow v_i=0]\Rightarrow[\widehat T_C(\bar x)\supset\bigcap_i\widehat T_{C_i}(\bar x),\ N_C(\bar x)\subset\sum_iN_{C_i}(\bar x)];\quad [\forall i,\ C_i\text{ regular at }\bar x]\Rightarrow[C\text{ regular},\ T_C=\bigcap_iT_{C_i},\ N_C=\sum_iN_{C_i}].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Clarke Regularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent primal, dual, polarity, and continuity criteria at a locally closed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\). The following are equivalent: \(N_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x)\); \(T_C(\bar x)=\widehat T_C(\bar x)\); \(N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^*\); \(T_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)^*\); \(\langle v,w\rangle\le0\) for every \(v\in N_C(\bar x)\) and \(w\in T_C(\bar x)\); \(\widehat N_C\) is osc at \(\bar x\) relative to \(C\); and \(T_C\) is sc at \(\bar x\) relative to \(C\). Any of these conditions means that \(C\) is Clarke regular at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a locally closed point, Clarke regularity is equivalently equality of limiting and regular normals, equality of general and regular tangents, mutual polarity of the tangent and normal cones, nonpositive pairing of every tangent with every normal, outer semicontinuity of the regular-normal mapping, or semicontinuity of the tangent mapping relative to the set.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is locally closed at }\bar x
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_C(\bar x)=\widehat N_C(\bar x)\iff T_C(\bar x)=\widehat T_C(\bar x)\iff N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^*\iff T_C(\bar x)=N_C(\bar x)^*\iff \forall(v,w)\in N_C(\bar x)\times T_C(\bar x),\ \langle v,w\rangle\le0\iff \widehat N_C\text{ is osc relative to }C\iff T_C\text{ is sc relative to }C

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangents and normals to finite product sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional formulas for closed product sets, including the regularity boundary for equality of contingent tangents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C=\prod_{i=1}^m C_i\subset\prod_{i=1}^m\mathbb R^{n_i}, where every C_i is closed, and let \bar x=(\bar x_1,\ldots,\bar x_m)\in C. Then N_C(\bar x)=\prod_{i=1}^mN_{C_i}(\bar x_i), \widehat N_C(\bar x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x_i), T_C(\bar x)\subset\prod_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(\bar x_i), and \widehat T_C(\bar x)=\prod_{i=1}^m\widehat T_{C_i}(\bar x_i). Moreover, C is regular at \bar x iff every C_i is regular at \bar x_i; in that case T_C(\bar x)=\prod_{i=1}^mT_{C_i}(\bar x_i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite product of closed sets, limiting and regular normal cones factor componentwise, regular tangent cones factor componentwise, and contingent tangents are contained in the product of the component tangents. The product is regular exactly when every factor is regular, and then the tangent inclusion is equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_C(\bar x)=\prod_iN_{C_i}(\bar x_i),\quad \widehat N_C(\bar x)=\prod_i\widehat N_{C_i}(\bar x_i),\quad T_C(\bar x)\subset\prod_iT_{C_i}(\bar x_i),\quad \widehat T_C(\bar x)=\prod_i\widehat T_{C_i}(\bar x_i),\quad [C\text{ regular at }\bar x\iff \forall i,\ C_i\text{ regular at }\bar x_i],\text{ with tangent equality in the regular case}.

children.title: Limiting Polarity Regime

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(\bar x)=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_C\bar x}\widehat N_C(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional outer-limit construction of nonconvex limiting normals.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The limiting normal cone is the outer limit of regular normal cones:
\[N_C(\bar x):=\operatorname*{Limsup}_{x\to_C\bar x}\widehat N_C(x)=\left\{x^*: \exists x_k\to_C\bar x,\ \exists x_k^*\to x^*,\ x_k^*\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\right\}.\]
Unlike \(\widehat N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ\), this cone records normals generated at nearby points. Consequently it can be nonconvex and need not equal the polar of the contingent tangent cone at \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting normal is a limit of regular normals at nearby feasible points, and the resulting cone may be nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Polarity Regime

children.title: Convexified Polarity Regime
children.top_down_role: Polarity behavior after passage to Clarke-type convexified constructions.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}N_C(\bar x)=T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clarke convexification restores exact tangent–normal polarity.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the Clarke normal cone by convexifying the limiting normal cone:
\[N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x):=\overline{\operatorname{co}}N_C(\bar x).\]
For the Clarke tangent cone \(T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\), exact polarity is recovered:
\[N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)^\circ,\qquad T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)^\circ.\]
Both cones are closed and convex. Convexification can strictly enlarge the limiting normal cone and can strictly shrink the contingent tangent cone when \(C\) is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying limiting normals produces the Clarke normal cone, which is exactly polar to the Clarke tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexified Polarity Regime

children.title: Limiting-to-Clarke Polarity Passage
children.top_down_role: Structural changes in dual geometry caused by convexification.

assumptions_latex: \(C\subset X\) is locally closed at \(\bar x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C(\bar x)\subset N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Passage from limiting normals to Clarke polar geometry by closed convexification.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The passage from limiting to Clarke geometry is
\[N_C(\bar x)\subset N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x):=\overline{\operatorname{co}}N_C(\bar x),\qquad T_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)^\circ.\]
Thus closed convexification removes the nonconvex directional distinctions retained by limiting normals and yields a cone admitting exact polarity. The inclusion is an equality whenever the limiting normal cone is already closed and convex, in particular under Clarke regularity where the regular and limiting normal cones coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed convexification carries limiting normals into Clarke geometry and restores an exact polar tangent cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Limiting-to-Clarke Polarity Passage

children.title: Nonconvex Polarity Gaps
children.top_down_role: Regimes where exact convex polarity analogies cease to represent local branch geometry.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T_C(\bar x)^\circ=\{0\}\subsetneq N_C(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cross-shaped set exhibiting strict gaps among regular, limiting, and Clarke polarity.

source_refs.locator: B. Normal Cones and Clarke Regularity p. 199

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the union of the coordinate axes at the origin,
\[T_C(\bar x)=C,\qquad \widehat N_C(\bar x)=T_C(\bar x)^\circ=\{0\}.\]
Normals obtained along either punctured axis give
\[N_C(\bar x)=C,\qquad N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}C=\mathbb R^2.\]
Hence \(T_C(\bar x)^\circ=\{0\}\subsetneq N_C(\bar x)\subsetneq N_C^{\mathrm C}(\bar x)\). This concrete nonconvex set shows why limiting normals are not generally polar to contingent tangents and why Clarke convexification loses directional separation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two crossing lines, the tangent polar is zero, limiting normals form the two lines, and Clarke normals fill the plane.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Polarity Gaps

children.title: Nearest-Point Normal Geometry
children.top_down_role: Normal information generated by local and global projections.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y-x\in N_C^P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal information generated by an attained nearest-point projection.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(x\in P_C(y)\), then comparison of squared distances gives
\[\langle y-x,z-x\rangle\leq\frac12\|z-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.\]
Consequently \(y-x\in N_C^P(x)\). If \(y\notin C\), the normalized direction \((y-x)/\|y-x\|\) is a nonzero unit proximal normal. The assertion is conditional on attainment of the distance; a general nonconvex closed subset of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space need not admit a nearest point for every \(y\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Whenever a nearest point exists, the displacement from it to the external point is a proximal normal.
knowledge_statements.title: Nearest-Point Normal Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Normal-Map Equivalence for a Box MCP
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the box normal map, gives the two-way solution transformation, and records regularity and feasible evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=[a,b]\) and \(F:\mathbb R^m\to\mathbb R^m\), define the normal map \[F_C(z)=F(P_C(z))+z-P_C(z).\] Then \[F_C(z)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad u=P_C(z)\text{ solves the box MCP},\] with the inverse correspondence \(z=u-F(u)\) for every MCP solution \(u\). If \(F\) is \(C^k\), then \(F_C\) is piecewise \(C^k\). Moreover, \(F\) is evaluated only at the feasible point \(P_C(z)\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The normal map adds the projection correction to F evaluated at the projected point. Its zeros correspond exactly to box-MCP solutions through u = P_C(z) and z = u − F(u). It inherits piecewise smoothness from F and never evaluates F outside the box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_C(z)=0\iff u=P_C(z)\text{ solves the MCP},\qquad z=u-F(u)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distance-attaining points generate normalized proximal normals.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(d_C(y):=\inf_{z\in C}\|y-z\|\). If \(x\in P_C(y)\) and \(y\notin C\), then
\[d_C(y)=\|y-x\|>0,\qquad u:=\frac{y-x}{d_C(y)}\in N_C^P(x),\qquad\|u\|=1.\]
Moreover, for every \(z\in C\),
\[\langle u,z-x\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2d_C(y)}\|z-x\|^2.\]
Thus an attained distance value determines both a nearest boundary point and a normalized proximal supporting direction there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained positive distance identifies a nearest point and a unit proximal normal pointing toward the external point.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance-Function Geometry

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in P_C(x+ru)\iff B(x+ru,r)\cap C=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: open ball of radius r centered at a

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent projection and supporting-ball representations of a proximal-normal direction.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Variational Geometry p. 196

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The open ball centered at \(x+ru\) with radius \(r\) supports \(C\) at \(x\) exactly when
\[B(x+ru,r)\cap C=\varnothing.\]
Because \(\|x-(x+ru)\|=r\), this condition is equivalent to \(x\in P_C(x+ru)\). In that case \(u\in N_C^P(x)\), with \(r\) serving as a proximal-support parameter, and
\[\langle u,z-x\rangle\leq\frac{1}{2r}\|z-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radius-r open ball centered at x+ru avoids the set and touches it at x exactly when x is a nearest point to the center; this makes u a proximal normal supported with radius r.
knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Ball Geometry

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(v\in\mathbb R^n\), one has \(v\in N_C^P(x)\) exactly when there exists \(r>0\) such that \(x\in P_C(x+rv)\). Equivalently, there exists \(\sigma\geq0\) such that \[\langle v,y-x\rangle\leq \sigma\|y-x\|^2\qquad\text{for every }y\in C.\] Thus a proximal normal is precisely a direction generated by a nearest-point relation, or equivalently by quadratic support of the set at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Singularities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary medial-axis singularity exhibiting both projection nonuniqueness and selection instability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{(-1,0),(1,0)\}\subset\mathbb R^2\), the metric projection satisfies \[P_C(0,0)=C.\] Every single-valued selection \(p:\mathbb R^2\to C\) with \(p(y)\in P_C(y)\) for all \(y\in\mathbb R^2\) is discontinuous at \((0,0)\). Thus the perpendicular bisector is a projection-singularity locus.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two isolated points, projection is nonunique on their perpendicular bisector, and every globally defined nearest-point selection is discontinuous at the origin.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a closed set \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) and \(x\in C\), the normal constructions satisfy \[N_C^P(x)\subset\widehat N_C(x)\subset N_C(x)\subset N_C^C(x).\] The limiting cone admits the sequential representation \[N_C(x)=\{v:\exists x_k\to_C x,\ v_k\to v,\ v_k\in\widehat N_C(x_k)\},\] and the Clarke normal cone satisfies \[N_C^C(x)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}N_C(x).\] The limiting cone can retain nonconvex branch-sensitive data that is lost under Clarke convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Proximal normals lie inside regular normals, which lie inside limiting normals; closing and convexifying the limiting cone produces the Clarke normal cone and may erase branch-sensitive data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_C^P(x)\subset\widehat N_C(x)\subset N_C(x)\subset N_C^C(x)=\overline{\operatorname{co}}N_C(x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Limiting normal cone and its closure boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential construction of limiting normals from proximal normals, including the distinct convexity and closedness properties of the two cones.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For x\in S, define
\[
N_S^L(x):=\left\{\zeta:\exists\,x_i\in S,\ \zeta_i\in N_S^P(x_i),\ x_i\to x,\ \zeta_i\to\zeta\right\}.
\]
The cone \(N_S^P(x)\) is convex but need not be closed, whereas \(N_S^L(x)\) is closed but need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For x in S, the limiting normal cone consists of limits of proximal normals at points of S converging to x. The proximal normal cone is always convex but may fail to be closed; the limiting normal cone is always closed but may fail to be convex.
